Install this before the matching portal update, or with it. Adds per-customer scope to the on-demand Azure sweep so the portal's new Sweep Azure now button reads one customer rather than every customer, and refuses a second sweep of the same customer while one is still running.

A sweep that found nothing to do now says why, instead of returning a bare zero: no Azure connection yet, a connection that is not connected, a customer whose seat is not active, or a connection made in the last five minutes that Azure Resource Graph has not caught up with.

The two on-demand sweep endpoints are now guarded by the backend itself rather than by the way the deployment happens to be configured. They were protected only by the sign-in layer in front of the Function App; a deployment configured without it would have had no protection at all, and the sweep's response names customers' subscriptions.

Fixes a false “could not be read” on the Azure posture card. A tenant whose Azure score history had not been written yet — which is every tenant until its first Azure sweep after the previous update — made the assessment document print that the history could not be read and that this was a fault on our side. It was not: there was simply nothing there yet. An empty history now reads as an empty history, and a genuinely failed read still says so. A tenant that has already been swept was never affected, and any tenant that shows the wrong panel today is corrected by its next sweep with or without this update.
Backend only. Your portal is unchanged by this release and needs no update alongside it.

Keeps a durable record of what closed. A daily per-tenant score is snapshotted per category, and every finding that stops firing leaves a dated Resolution saying why it closed — fixed, the check retired, or the tenant offboarded. A check that could not be evaluated no longer closes its finding as resolved, so a licence gap or a failed read is never reported to a customer as work they completed.

All 69 checks now live in one registry that is validated when the service starts, and each one states what it measures and where its bar sits. Findings and priced opportunities cite the checks behind them. Two checks were retitled and one dropped from medium to low in that pass, so scores move slightly on the next sweep for a reason on our side — which is exactly the movement the portal's documents now mark on the trend.
Install this before or with the portal update.

Splits the case where an opportunity's evidence can no longer be read, by whether the project was won. A won one stays in the resolved list and keeps its price; anything still open goes back into the active pipeline with no derived value. Previously both went to the resolved list, so a deal an operator was working migrated into history because a sweep failed.

A row whose evidence could not be re-read no longer reports an outcome that claims the evidence cleared. It reports the delivery it can stand behind and flags the unreadable evidence separately, so nothing downstream has to infer the difference from one field.
Install the portal update first, or with this one. On its own, an older portal renders a won project whose evidence went dark as a plain Delivered with its evidence cleared.

Serves a written scope sentence for every included-scope line on an opportunity, instead of leaving the portal to assemble one from the observation text. The field is required, so a new opportunity type cannot ship a scope line the proposal has no wording for — it fails to build rather than reaching a customer as broken prose.

Operator-facing evidence on the Conditional Access baseline now names Guard. Two lines read as observations about the customer's Microsoft tenant when both were describing Guard's own state on our side — one had already been mistaken for a tenant misconfiguration and written into a draft proposal as one.
Install this before or with the portal update. The portal degrades gracefully without it rather than breaking, but the proposal scope lines it prints are the unfixed ones.

Serves the pending Microsoft 365 invite that the Customers list reads. Install this before the portal update — the portal shows the field either way, but until this is in place an address typed there is accepted and never recorded. When a customer approves, their invite is matched against every domain their tenant has verified rather than only its default one, and cleared automatically, because an operator who wrote to admin@customer.com has named a domain that is frequently not the one the directory reports first.

A customer you have lost access to is named again, rather than shown as a bare identifier. Reading a customer's name relies on a permission that deliberately sits outside the set your customers are asked to approve — it is not on their consent screen, and should not be. The side effect was that approving consent in your own tenant quietly removed it again each time, so a disconnected customer could come back as a long identifier with nothing to say which one it was. That permission is now checked and put back automatically: once straight after a consent is approved, and once more on the nightly sweep, so it repairs itself whether it went missing through a consent or was removed by hand. Nothing about what your customers approve has changed, and no new credential is created in the process.

Install this before the portal release of the same date. It adds the portfolio-wide Azure rollup that the new Azure page reads — against an older backend that page opens empty, with nothing saying why.

Won projects now keep the price they were actually agreed at. A project won three months ago held only a figure recalculated from today's evidence and today's rate card, so what you had sold appeared to move on its own; the agreed price is now carried alongside it.

Install this before the portal release of the same date. That release totals won work per customer and reads this price to do it — against an older backend those totals come out short, with no sign that anything is missing.

Upgrading a customer to the root management group now tidies up after itself. When a customer who connected Azure one subscription at a time re-opens the invite as someone with rights at the root management group, Basewiser removes the narrower Reader assignment it no longer needs — so their Access control (IAM) shows one Basewiser assignment instead of two, and a security reviewer looking at it does not have to work out why there were ever two.

This is the only thing Basewiser ever deletes in a customer's tenant, and it is deliberately narrow. It removes only the assignment Basewiser itself wrote, only during the invite the customer has just approved, and only after confirming the wider access actually works — so it can never take away access the customer still needs. If the removal is refused, the assignment is left exactly where it is and the connection window says so; it grants nothing beyond what the root management group already covers.

Re-checking access no longer records scopes it could not verify. When "Re-check access in Azure" could not reach Azure to ask about the root management group, it recorded the narrower per-subscription scopes as though it had checked them. It now records nothing when it cannot answer, which is what the rest of the re-check already did.

The Azure pages in your portal read this. Findings from the nightly sweep are now served joined to the subscriptions and resources they belong to, and written in plain language rather than check names — so the new Azure section has something to show. Update the backend as well as the portal, or those pages will be empty.

A connection that was only ever half-granted now reports itself as one. The subscriptions that were visible when the customer approved Azure and were never granted are named, along with the role-assignment command that completes them, so the portal can stop calling a half-monitored customer finished.

Setting up the Basewiser app now removes the client secret it replaces. Every attempt to retire an old one had been refused by Entra and quietly ignored, so a customer's app registration could accumulate up to three live two-year credentials. It now retries the removal and confirms it, and it will tidy the ones already there on the next setup.

Basewiser now scans your customers' Azure. Twenty-four checks run every night at 01:00 UTC against the read-only access a customer granted when they connected Azure — public exposure, encryption and transport, Azure role assignments, Defender coverage, logging, and resources you are paying for and not using. No portal update is needed and nothing changes on the customer's Azure bill; the sweep only reads.

You will not see the findings yet. There is no Azure section in the portal in this release — this update starts the nightly collection so the pages have real history to show the day they arrive. Nothing for you to do.

One thing does surface now. A customer's Azure subscription Owners are checked against their Microsoft 365 multi-factor registration, so an account holding Owner with no MFA registered appears under Opportunities by name, with the subscriptions it holds.
Install this together with the portal release of the same date.

Re-activating the Basewiser app is now safe to repeat. It finds your app by its application ID rather than its name, so renaming it in Entra can no longer create a duplicate alongside the one your customers approved.
Each re-activation used to leave its old client secret valid for two years. The secrets it replaces are now removed; any you created yourself are left alone.
